A bioprinter comprises one or more dispensing units. The microtissue may comprise cartilage cells or tumor cells or liver cells.

A bioprinter includes one or more dispensing units configured to dispense a bioink. Each dispensing unit may be arranged to hold and deliver a selected bioink in a controlled manner during a printing process.

In some embodiments, each dispensing unit includes a syringe, a plunger, an actuator, a controller, and a nozzle. The syringe includes a syringe body configured to contain the bioink. The syringe body has an exit orifice through which the bioink may be discharged. The plunger is positioned within the syringe body and is movable to apply pressure to the bioink. Movement of the plunger is driven by the actuator, which is operably connected to the controller. The controller regulates operation of the actuator, thereby controlling movement of the plunger and the dispensing of bioink from the syringe.

The nozzle is coupled to the syringe body and defines a fluid path extending from an inlet of the nozzle to an outlet of the nozzle. The nozzle is connected to the exit orifice of the syringe so that bioink discharged from the syringe can enter the nozzle and flow through the fluid path to the nozzle outlet. The nozzle may also be connected to a fluid source, allowing an additional fluid to be introduced into the nozzle or combined with the bioink before or during dispensing.

In use, the bioprinter may be operated to prepare microtissue by dispensing bioink onto a plate or other receiving surface. The bioink may include biological material such as cells, extracellular matrix components, hydrogels, nutrients, or other suitable materials for supporting cell growth or tissue formation. The cells may include, for example, cartilage cells, tumor cells, or liver cells. By controlling the dispensing units, the bioprinter can deposit the bioink in predetermined locations and patterns on the plate, thereby forming microtissue structures suitable for research, testing, screening, or tissue-engineering applications.
outputs.L4:
A bioprinter can be configured to prepare microtissues by dispensing small, controlled volumes of bioink onto a receiving surface, such as a culture plate, well plate, substrate, or other suitable support. The system may include one or more syringe-based dispensing units, each containing a bioink composition. Each dispensing unit typically includes a syringe barrel, a plunger, and a nozzle. The plunger is driven by an actuator, such as a motorized linear actuator, pneumatic actuator, or other controllable drive mechanism, so that the bioink can be extruded with precision through the nozzle.

The nozzles are connected to fluid pathways that guide the bioink from the syringe barrels to the dispensing outlets. These pathways may be designed to maintain sterility, reduce dead volume, and allow accurate delivery of bioink droplets, strands, or defined patterns. By controlling parameters such as plunger displacement, dispensing pressure, nozzle diameter, flow rate, printing speed, and deposition location, the bioprinter can place the bioink in predetermined arrangements on the plate. This makes it possible to form microtissues with controlled size, shape, composition, and spatial organization.

The bioink may include living cells suspended in a biocompatible material, such as a hydrogel precursor, extracellular matrix material, or other cell-supportive medium. After dispensing, the printed material may be stabilized or crosslinked by chemical, thermal, ionic, enzymatic, or light-based methods, depending on the composition of the bioink. The resulting structures can provide a three-dimensional environment that supports cell viability, proliferation, differentiation, and tissue-like organization.

This type of bioprinting system is suitable for fabricating microtissues containing many different cell types. For example, cartilage cells or chondrocytes may be printed to create cartilage-like constructs for studying joint disease, repair strategies, or regenerative medicine approaches. Tumor cells may be printed alone or together with stromal, immune, or vascular cells to generate cancer models for drug screening and tumor biology studies. Liver cells, including hepatocytes and supporting non-parenchymal cells, may be used to form liver microtissues for toxicity testing, metabolism studies, and disease modeling.

Because the dispensing process can be automated and precisely controlled, the system can produce multiple microtissues in a repeatable manner. This is useful for high-throughput experiments, where many similar tissue constructs are needed for testing different compounds, culture conditions, or genetic backgrounds. The ability to control the position and amount of deposited bioink also enables the fabrication of more complex tissue models, including layered structures, patterned co-cultures, and microtissues with defined cellular architectures.

Overall, the bioprinter provides a versatile platform for producing cell-containing microtissues for tissue engineering and biomedical research. By combining syringe-based dispensing, actuator-controlled extrusion, and programmable deposition onto a plate, the system enables reproducible fabrication of three-dimensional biological constructs. These microtissues can be used to investigate tissue development, disease mechanisms, drug responses, toxicity, and potential therapeutic strategies.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a patent-style abstract for a bioprinter with syringe dispensing units, actuators, controller, nozzle fluid paths, and use in preparing microtissues from bioink on a plate.
counterfactuals.output: A bioprinter for preparing microtissues includes a support configured to receive a plate, one or more syringe dispensing units configured to contain and dispense a bioink, and one or more actuators operably coupled to the syringe dispensing units. Each syringe dispensing unit includes a nozzle defining a fluid path from a syringe reservoir to an outlet positioned to dispense the bioink onto or into selected locations of the plate. A controller is configured to control relative positioning between the outlet and the plate and to operate the actuators to dispense predetermined volumes or patterns of the bioink through the fluid paths. The bioink may include cells and a matrix material, such that dispensing the bioink onto the plate forms discrete deposits or structures that develop or are processed into microtissues. The controller may execute instructions to coordinate dispensing from multiple syringe dispensing units, adjust dispensing parameters, and generate arrays of microtissues having selected compositions, dimensions, or spatial arrangements.

An invention is provided for a bioprinter apparatus and associated method for fabricating microtissue constructs. The apparatus includes one or more dispensing units, each dispensing unit comprising a syringe configured to contain a bioink or cell-containing material, a plunger received within the syringe, an actuator operably coupled to the plunger to control extrusion, a controller configured to regulate actuator movement and dispensing parameters, and a nozzle in fluid communication with the syringe for depositing the material onto a receiving surface or into a culture vessel.

In operation, the controller coordinates movement of the actuator and/or dispensing unit to deliver controlled volumes of bioink through the nozzle according to a predetermined print pattern. The apparatus may include multiple dispensing units to sequentially or simultaneously deposit different cell types, hydrogels, extracellular matrix components, growth factors, or support materials. Printing parameters such as extrusion rate, pressure, nozzle position, layer height, and deposition sequence may be adjusted to form three-dimensional microtissue structures.

A method of printing microtissue includes loading at least one syringe with a bioink comprising viable cells, positioning the nozzle relative to a substrate or well, actuating the plunger under controller command to dispense the bioink, and depositing the bioink in a defined pattern to generate a microtissue construct. The printed construct may be cultured under conditions suitable for cell viability, maturation, or tissue-specific function. Exemplary microtissues include cartilage microtissue comprising chondrocytes or stem-cell-derived cartilage cells, tumor microtissue comprising cancer cells alone or with stromal cells, and liver microtissue comprising hepatocytes, hepatic progenitor cells, endothelial cells, or supporting cells. The apparatus and method enable reproducible fabrication of small-scale tissue models for research, drug screening, disease modeling, and regenerative medicine applications.

counterfactuals.prompt: Please describe, in formal patent language, a bioprinter that includes a syringe-based dispensing unit connected to a nozzle and fluid passageway, and explain how it may be used to make cell-containing microtissue.
counterfactuals.output:
A bioprinting apparatus is provided, comprising a syringe-based dispensing unit configured to receive and dispense a biological composition, the dispensing unit including a syringe barrel defining an interior reservoir, a plunger movably disposed within the syringe barrel, and an actuator operably coupled to the plunger for applying a controlled dispensing force. The syringe-based dispensing unit is fluidly coupled to a nozzle by a fluid passageway, wherein the fluid passageway is configured to convey the biological composition from the interior reservoir of the syringe barrel to an outlet of the nozzle.

In some embodiments, the nozzle is removably coupled to the fluid passageway and includes an orifice sized to extrude a continuous filament, droplet, or discrete volume of the biological composition. The fluid passageway may comprise a conduit, connector, manifold, or channel extending between the syringe barrel and the nozzle, and may be configured to reduce dead volume, maintain sterility, and preserve viability of cells suspended within the biological composition. The dispensing unit may be mounted on a positioning assembly configured to move the nozzle relative to a build surface in one, two, or three dimensions. Alternatively, the build surface may be movable relative to the nozzle.

The biological composition may comprise a bioink including living cells dispersed within a hydrogel precursor, extracellular matrix material, polymeric carrier, culture medium, crosslinkable material, or combinations thereof. Suitable cells may include, without limitation, stem cells, progenitor cells, differentiated mammalian cells, endothelial cells, fibroblasts, epithelial cells, immune cells, tumor cells, or combinations thereof.

In operation, the biological composition is loaded into the syringe barrel of the dispensing unit. The actuator advances the plunger to force the biological composition through the fluid passageway and out of the nozzle. The nozzle and/or build surface is moved according to a predetermined deposition pattern, thereby depositing the biological composition in a selected geometry. The deposited material may be crosslinked, gelled, cured, or otherwise stabilized during or after deposition, for example by ionic crosslinking, thermal gelation, photopolymerization, enzymatic reaction, pH change, or contact with a crosslinking solution.

The apparatus may be used to fabricate a cell-containing microtissue by dispensing one or more volumes or filaments of the cell-containing biological composition onto or into a receiving substrate, mold, well plate, culture chamber, support bath, or previously deposited layer. The dispensed composition is arranged to define a microtissue having a predetermined size, shape, cellular distribution, and/or architecture. Following deposition, the microtissue is maintained under culture conditions sufficient to support cell viability, attachment, proliferation, differentiation, self-assembly, matrix remodeling, or tissue maturation. In some embodiments, multiple cell-containing compositions are dispensed sequentially or concurrently to form a heterogeneous microtissue comprising spatially patterned cell populations.

Accordingly, the bioprinter enables controlled dispensing of a cell-laden material from a syringe reservoir through a fluid passageway and nozzle, allowing reproducible manufacture of cell-containing microtissues suitable for tissue engineering, disease modeling, drug screening, regenerative medicine research, or biological assay applications.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an abstract for a biomedical printing invention involving one or more syringe/nozzle dispensing units controlled by actuators to deposit bioink onto a plate for forming microtissues.
counterfactuals.output: A biomedical printing system for forming microtissues includes one or more syringe or nozzle dispensing units configured to retain and dispense a bioink onto a receiving plate or substrate. Each dispensing unit is operably coupled to one or more actuators configured to control dispensing parameters, including position, displacement, flow rate, pressure, and/or deposition timing. A controller coordinates movement of the dispensing units and actuation of the syringes or nozzles according to a predetermined or dynamically adjustable print pattern to deposit controlled volumes of bioink at selected locations on the plate. The deposited bioink may include living cells, extracellular matrix materials, hydrogels, growth factors, and/or other biological components suitable for forming microtissues. The system enables reproducible fabrication of arrays or patterned arrangements of microtissues for biological assays, tissue engineering, drug screening, disease modeling, or regenerative medicine applications.
